The Quechua. The largest indigenous people of South America and direct descendants of the Inca Empire, inhabiting the Andean highlands across multiple nations and maintaining rich traditions of mountain agriculture and distinctive textiles. The Quechua inhabit the Andes mountains and surrounding regions across multiple South American nations, with the largest concentrations in Peru and Bolivia. They speak Quechua languages, with multiple varieties including Quichua and Kichwa, descended from the Inca lingua franca. Over eight million speakers remain, making Quechua the most widely spoken indigenous language in the Americas. As direct descendants of the Inca Empire, which they ruled until Spanish conquest in fifteen thirty-two, the Quechua preserve continuities with Inca traditions in agriculture, governance, and spirituality. They practice terrace farming on steep Andean slopes, cultivating potatoes, quinoa, maize, and other Andean crops. They developed sophisticated agricultural knowledge and preservation techniques like chuño, freeze-dried potatoes that can last for years. The Quechua create distinctive woven textiles including aguayos, ponchos, and chullos using traditional techniques and natural dyes. These textiles encode identity, community affiliation, and regional variation. Many rural Quechua communities maintain ayllu organization, a system of reciprocal labor exchange and kinship-based social units that predates and survived the Inca period. Their spiritual traditions blend animism with Catholicism, revering Apus, or mountain spirits, and Pachamama, the earth mother. Traditional ceremonies honor these sacred relationships.
